A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Disease-Aware Prompting (DAP) work. Their main sections, equations, tables, and figures can be matched reliably. v1 ends after the references; v2 adds readable Appendices A–F. No material reading gaps prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original grounding benchmarks on MS-CXR, RSNA Pneumonia, and COVID Rural, together with token-alignment analyses and component ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds hyperparameter studies, interpretability-map robustness experiments, and 20-shot fine-tuning results.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same interpretability-map feature weighting, global and local contrastive losses, Dice supervision, decoder, and inference procedure. The appendix evaluates alternative configurations and fine-tuning settings without specifying a replacement core algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use MIMIC-CXR for training and MS-CXR, RSNA Pneumonia, and COVID Rural for grounding evaluation. The added experiments vary supervision, hyperparameters, and training-map quality on these existing datasets; they introduce no additional dataset, disease domain, or grounding task.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in the main benchmark and prompt-comparison tables remain unchanged. Appendix B.3, Table 8 adds evaluated GradCAM, SmoothGrad, and LRP variants as alternative interpretability-map generators within DAP, compared with the original Chefer-based configuration and Self-EQ.

E3.justification: The appendix adds substantial experimental protocols: 20-shot dense-label fine-tuning, controlled removal of important prompt-map pixels followed by retraining, and sweeps over batch size, learning rate, loss weights, prompting depth, and prompt count. Appendix B.1 also specifies a learning rate of 0.001 for other experiments, without reconciling Section 4's retained 0.008. This does not establish that the original benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained token and component analyses, Appendices A, B, and E directly examine whether DAP improves its initial interpretability maps, sensitivity to multiple hyperparameters, dependence on the interpretability method, and degradation under deliberately corrupted maps. These substantially extend the evidence about how and when DAP works.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new scatterplots and grouped averages describe sample-level performance rather than introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The main results in Tables 1–4 remain unchanged, while Tables 5–11 and Figures 13–17 add substantial numerical and qualitative evidence. For example, Table 11 newly reports RSNA 20-shot DAP results of 1.741 CNR and 0.551 Dice, alongside the retained weakly supervised values of 1.630 and 0.474. These are results under additional training conditions, not improvements to the original same-setting scores.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, prompting equations, contrastive-loss definitions, and total objective remain unchanged. The appendix adds empirical studies without new theorems, proofs, formal assumptions, or mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and shortened conclusion retain the same claims about excessive background-token norms, global–local misalignment, annotation-free DAP training, benchmark novelty, and the reported 20.74% improvement. The appendix supplies additional supporting evidence without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix E adds a concrete qualification: DAP depends on interpretability-map quality and can fall below g++ under heavy artificial corruption. Appendix B adds interpretations concerning prompt diversity, prompting depth, and loss weighting. These refine the retained background-suppression and alignment explanation rather than replacing it.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly supplies the GPT-4o generation instruction, including exclusion of anatomical locations. Appendix B identifies the 20% MS-CXR tuning subset and tested parameter settings, while Appendix E specifies the corruption threshold and removal fractions. These improve documentation, although the relationship between the appendix and main-text learning rates remains unclear.

R1.justification: Section 2 revises its grounding-method taxonomy and adds discussion of RefCLIP, QueryMatch, and grounded medical multimodal LLMs. v2 also adds a concept-based medical-image reasoning citation and removes several auxiliary-task references. These are targeted positioning updates; the principal novelty claim remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the grounding-related-work paragraph, trims the introduction and conclusion, makes local wording corrections, updates an affiliation, and organizes supplementary material into Appendices A–F. Most main-text prose and the section sequence remain stable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–11 and Figures 13–17, introducing hyperparameter tables, map-quality diagnostics, corruption plots, a weak-versus-20-shot comparison, and two full-page qualitative galleries. Figure 2 is also relocated within the introduction. This substantially expands the visual presentation while retaining the original main displays.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the paper by directly testing sensitivity to the quality and source of its interpretability maps, documenting failure under corruption, and providing the text-generation instruction. These additions make the retained method and results better supported. The gain is limited by unresolved reporting ambiguity, particularly Appendix B.1's 0.001 learning rate versus Section 4's 0.008, which prevents a fully consistent reproduction recipe.
